title: Operation Flash: The Dress Rehearsal for Storm
sources: ICTY Gotovina et al. Trial Judgment (IT-06-90-T)
content:
On the morning of 1 May 1995, the Croatian Army launched Operation Flash against the Western Slavonia sector of the Republic of Serbian Krajina. The offensive lasted barely thirty-six hours. By 2 May, Croatian forces had overrun the entire enclave, scattering its defenders and reestablishing Croatian authority over a territory that had been outside Zagreb's control since 1991. The operation was small in scale compared to what would follow three months later, but its significance extended far beyond the territory it recaptured.

Western Slavonia was the smallest and most vulnerable of the four United Nations Protected Areas established in 1992 under the Vance Plan, which had frozen the front lines of the 1991 Croatian War of Independence. UNSCR 981, adopted in March 1995, had reauthorized the UN peacekeeping operation in Croatia under a new name — the United Nations Confidence Restoration Operation — but the fundamental problem remained unchanged. The Krajina Serb authorities rejected Croatian sovereignty, and the UN presence served primarily to maintain a status quo that Croatia found increasingly intolerable. Western Slavonia's geographic isolation, separated from the main Krajina territory around Knin by a wide band of Croatian-controlled land, made it militarily indefensible.

The Croatian attack was swift and well-coordinated. Multiple brigade-strength formations advanced along converging axes, overwhelming the local SVK garrison before reinforcement or organized retreat was possible. The operation demonstrated the transformation of the Croatian military from the poorly equipped territorial defense forces of 1991 into a reorganized, trained, and disciplined conventional army.

The Krajina Serb response revealed both desperation and the limitations of the Serbian strategic position. Unable to mount a military counter-offensive, the RSK and affiliated forces retaliated by firing Orkan rockets — a cluster munition system — at Zagreb on 2 and 3 May, killing seven civilians and wounding over a hundred. The attacks were militarily irrelevant to the situation in Western Slavonia but served as a warning of the consequences Croatia might face if it attempted similar operations against the larger Krajina heartland. The ICTY examined the broader context of Croatian military operations during this period in the Gotovina et al. case (IT-06-90-T), which focused primarily on the subsequent Operation Storm but addressed the strategic continuity between the two operations.

The international response to Operation Flash was notably muted. The UN Security Council issued statements expressing concern, but no meaningful action followed. The message was not lost on Zagreb: a rapid fait accompli that minimized civilian casualties and presented the international community with an accomplished fact would be tolerated. This lesson informed the planning for Operation Storm, which would be launched against the Krajina heartland on 4 August.

For the Bosnian Serbs, the fall of Western Slavonia carried immediate strategic implications. The RSK had served as a buffer and a symbol of the broader project of Serb territorial consolidation across the former Yugoslavia. Its progressive dismemberment signaled that Belgrade was unwilling or unable to guarantee the security of Serb communities outside Serbia proper. The VRS now faced a Croatian army that had demonstrated its willingness to use force decisively, positioned along the western flank of Bosnian Serb-held territory.

Operation Flash was, in retrospect, a dress rehearsal. It tested Croatian military capability, gauged the international reaction, and exposed the fragility of the Krajina Serb defensive position. Each of these lessons would be applied at vastly greater scale three months later when Operation Storm dismantled the Krajina Serb entity entirely and transformed the strategic balance of the Bosnian War.
